title: Equations, the mole and mole ratios
html:
Guiding question

How are chemical equations used to calculate reacting ratios?

R2.1.1 Chemical equations and mole ratios

A chemical equation shows the species taking part, their states and the proportions in which they react. Atoms can be combined or rearranged but never created or destroyed, so the total number of each type of atom stays constant. Reactants are used up and products formed in fixed mole ratios, given by the stoichiometric coefficients. For gases, the reacting volumes are in the same ratio.

An equation only shows the changes in amount. It does not tell you how much of each substance is present at the start or the end: one reactant may be in excess, or the reaction may not go to completion. The mole ratio can still be used to find any unknown quantity (amount, mass, volume) from a known one.

CodeUnderstanding
2.1.1Chemical equations show the ratio of reactants and products in a reaction.
2.1.2The mole ratio of an equation can be used to determine the masses and/or volumes of reactants and products, and the concentrations of reactants and products for reactions in solution.
2.1.3The limiting reactant determines the theoretical yield.
2.1.4The percentage yield is calculated from the ratio of experimental yield to theoretical yield.
2.1.5The atom economy is a measure of efficiency in green chemistry.

Stoichiometry

Stoichiometry is the quantitative study of the reactants and products in a reaction. If you know the reactants and products, you can write a balanced equation by adding stoichiometric coefficients so that the number of each type of atom is the same on both sides.

Worked example 1 · burning ethane C₂H₆ + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O (unbalanced)
Carbon: 2 on the left, so write 2 before CO₂. Hydrogen: 6 on the left, so write 3 before H₂O.
C₂H₆ + O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O
Oxygen: 7 on the right, so write 3.5 before O₂. Multiply everything by 2 for whole numbers, then add state symbols:
2C₂H₆(g) + 7O₂(g) → 4CO₂(g) + 6H₂O(l)
StateSymbol
solids
liquidl
gasg
aqueous solutionaq

Balance: __Fe2O3 + __CO → __Fe + __CO2. What are the coefficients?

  1. 1, 3, 2, 3
  2. 1, 1, 2, 1
  3. 2, 3, 4, 3
  4. 1, 2, 2, 2

Fe: 2 on the left, so 2Fe. O: 3 in Fe2O3; each CO takes one O to make CO2, so 3CO and 3CO2.

The mole ratio

The ratio of the stoichiometric coefficients is the mole ratio. Reactants always react in relative amounts equal to the mole ratio of the reactants, and produce relative amounts equal to the mole ratio of the products.

6CO₂(g) + 6H₂O(l) → C₆H₁₂O₆(aq) + 6O₂(g)

The reactants react 1 : 1 and the products form 1 : 6: equal amounts of CO₂ and water are used, producing six times less glucose than oxygen.

TOKOpen the Wikipedia article on stoichiometry in a language you don't know. You will still recognize the equations, diagrams and calculations. To what extent does a universal “language” like chemical equations help knowledge development?
Linking questionWhen is it useful to use half-equations? (Reactivity 3.2)
Use the mole ratios: 4Na + O2 → 2Na2O with 12 mol Na; 2Al + 3Cl2 → 2AlCl3 with 5 mol Al; C4H10 + 6½O2 → 4CO2 + 5H2O with 0.5 mol butane. Predict, then reveal

12 mol Na needs 3 mol O2 and makes 6 mol Na2O. 5 mol Al needs 7.5 mol Cl2 and makes 5 mol AlCl3. 0.5 mol butane needs 3.25 mol O2 and makes 2 mol CO2 and 2.5 mol H2O.

Counting particles by weighing

How could a bank count a large stack of identical banknotes using only a weighing scale? Weigh one note, weigh the stack, divide. Chemists count atoms the same way. Atoms are far too small and light to weigh one at a time, but if we know the mass of a very large, fixed number of them, we can count them by weighing. That fixed number is the mole: 6.02 × 1023 particles (the Avogadro constant, NA, in section 2 of the data booklet). Just as it is easier to count tubes of sweets than the individual sweets, it is easier to count moles than atoms.

The relative atomic mass, Ar, is the weighted average mass of the naturally occurring isotopes of an element relative to 1/12 of the mass of a carbon-12 atom; that is why chlorine is 35.45, not a whole number (a mixture of 35Cl and 37Cl). The relative formula mass, Mr, is the sum of the Ar values in the formula. The molar mass, M, has the same number with units g mol−1. In class we "add up the mass of the sheep": CO2 = 12.01 + 2(16.00) = 44.01.

n = m ÷ M N = n × NA

Calculate the molar mass of H2SO4.

2(1.01) + 32.07 + 4(16.00) = 98.09 g mol−1.

Calculate the molar mass of Co2(SO4)3.

2(58.93) + 3[32.07 + 4(16.00)] = 117.86 + 288.21 = 406.07 g mol−1 ≈ 406.1. Brackets multiply everything inside.

Mr race: LiI, CH4, HCl, NaCl, NH3, MgCl2, C6H12O6, Fe2O3, C4H10, KMnO4, Ni(CH3CO2)2, Na2HPO4. Work them out, then reveal

LiI 133.84; CH4 16.05; HCl 36.46; NaCl 58.44; NH3 17.04; MgCl2 95.21; C6H12O6 180.18; Fe2O3 159.70; C4H10 58.14; KMnO4 158.04; Ni(CH3CO2)2 176.79; Na2HPO4 141.96 g mol−1 (data-booklet Ar values; whole-number Ar values give 134, 16, 36.5, 58.5, 17, 95, 180, 160, 58, 158, 177, 142).

How many moles are in 193.2 g of magnesium carbonate, MgCO3?

M(MgCO3) = 24.31 + 12.01 + 48.00 = 84.32 g mol−1. n = 193.2 ÷ 84.32 = 2.29 mol.

How many water molecules are in 54.0 g of water?

n = 54.0 ÷ 18.02 = 3.00 mol. N = 3.00 × 6.02 × 1023 = 1.81 × 1024 molecules. (Type it as 1.81e24.)

title: Reacting masses
html:
R2.1.2 Reacting masses: the table method

Start with a puzzle: Mg + H2SO4 → MgSO4 + H2. If 24 g of magnesium makes 120 g of magnesium sulfate, how much MgSO4 would 12 g of magnesium make? You probably halved it without thinking. That instinct (amount of product is proportional to amount of reactant, through the mole ratio) is all a reacting-mass calculation is; the method below makes it reliable for any equation.

Write three rows (mass, M, mol) under the balanced equation and fill the gaps. Five steps:

  1. Balance the equation.
  2. Identify what you know and what you want to find.
  3. Convert the known mass to moles (n = m ÷ M).
  4. Use the mole ratio to find moles of the unknown.
  5. Convert moles back to mass (m = n × M).
Worked example · fireworksWhat mass of KNO₃ is needed to make 1.6 g of O₂? 2KNO₃ → 2KNO₂ + O₂
2KNO₃O₂
mass / g?1.6
M / g mol⁻¹101.1132.00
n / mol0.050 × 2 = 0.101.6 ÷ 32.00 = 0.050
mass KNO₃ = 0.10 × 101.11 = 10.1 g
Common mistakeDo not multiply the molar mass by the coefficient. M(FeCl₃) is 162.20 g mol⁻¹ whether the equation says FeCl₃ or 4FeCl₃. The coefficient is used only in the mole-ratio step.

In the table method, a student writes the molar mass of 2KNO3 as 202.22 g mol−1. What is wrong?

  1. Nothing: the coefficient must be included
  2. The molar mass is always for one formula unit (101.11); the coefficient is used only in the mole-ratio step
  3. Molar mass should be divided by the coefficient
  4. KNO3 has no molar mass

M(KNO3) = 101.11 g mol−1 whatever the coefficient. Using 2 × M and the 2 : 1 ratio would double-count the 2.

What mass of magnesium oxide is formed by complete combustion of 6.00 g of magnesium? 2Mg + O2 → 2MgO

n(Mg) = 6.00 ÷ 24.31 = 0.247 mol. Ratio Mg : MgO = 1 : 1, so n(MgO) = 0.247 mol. m = 0.247 × 40.30 = 9.95 g (10 g with whole-number Ar).

Copper(II) oxide is reduced by hydrogen: CuO + H2 → Cu + H2O. What mass of copper is obtained from 15.9 g of CuO?

n(CuO) = 15.9 ÷ 79.55 = 0.200 mol → 0.200 mol Cu → 0.200 × 63.55 = 12.7 g.

Fe + S → FeS. What mass of iron is needed to make 4.40 g of iron(II) sulfide?

n(FeS) = 4.40 ÷ 87.92 = 0.0500 mol → 0.0500 mol Fe → 0.0500 × 55.85 = 2.79 g (2.8 g).

6NO(g) + 4NH3(g) → 5N2(g) + 6H2O(g) removes NO from exhaust fumes. What mass of ammonia reacts with 18.0 g of NO?

n(NO) = 18.0 ÷ 30.01 = 0.600 mol. Ratio NO : NH3 = 6 : 4, so n(NH3) = 0.600 × 4/6 = 0.400 mol. m = 0.400 × 17.04 = 6.81 g.

Blast furnace: Fe2O3 + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO2. (a) What mass of Fe2O3 gives 112 g of iron? (b) How much iron comes from 320 tonnes of Fe2O3? (c) 320 tonnes of an impure ore makes 202 tonnes of iron: what is the percentage purity?

(a) n(Fe) = 112 ÷ 55.85 = 2.01 mol → 1.00 mol Fe2O3 → 160 g. (b) The mass ratio is the same in tonnes: 320 t ÷ 159.70 = 2.00 "tonne-moles" → 4.01 × 55.85 = 224 t. (c) 202 ÷ 224 × 100 = 90.2% pure. No need to convert tonnes to grams: the units cancel.

Practical: determining the composition of basic copper carbonate

"Basic copper carbonate" (the green solid in malachite and on weathered copper roofs) could be Cu2(OH)2CO3 or Cu3(OH)2(CO3)2. Reacting-mass ideas let you decide which.

  • Part 1, % CO2: weigh a conical flask, add about 0.15 g of sample and reweigh; add about 15 cm3 of HCl from a weighed measuring cylinder (reweigh the cylinder to find the mass of acid added). Copper carbonate + hydrochloric acid → copper chloride + carbon dioxide + water. When fizzing stops, swirl gently, then weigh the flask and contents. Mass lost = mass of CO2 released.
  • Part 2, % Cu: the concentration of the blue copper(II) solution is found by colorimetry: measure the absorbance at about 635 nm and read the concentration from a calibration graph made with standard copper(II) solutions.
  • Safety: HCl is corrosive and copper compounds are harmful if swallowed; wear eye protection and gloves and wash hands.
Predict: what % CO2 and % Cu would each formula give? Then reveal

Cu2(OH)2CO3: M = 221.13 g mol−1; CO2 = 44.01 ÷ 221.13 = 19.9%; Cu = 127.10 ÷ 221.13 = 57.5%.
Cu3(OH)2(CO3)2: M = 344.69 g mol−1; CO2 = 88.02 ÷ 344.69 = 25.5%; Cu = 190.65 ÷ 344.69 = 55.3%.
The % CO2 differs most, so Part 1 is the more decisive measurement. CO2 that stays dissolved makes the measured value too low.

Do now: a compound contains 32.65% S, 65.3% O and 2.04% H by mass. Find its empirical formula, then reveal

In 100 g: S 32.65 ÷ 32.07 = 1.018 mol; O 65.3 ÷ 16.00 = 4.08 mol; H 2.04 ÷ 1.01 = 2.02 mol. Divide by the smallest (1.018): S 1, O 4.01, H 1.98. Empirical formula H2SO4.

title: Limiting and excess reactants
html:
R2.1.3 Limiting and excess reactants

Think of making hot dogs: five sausages and three buns make only three hot dogs, however many sausages you have left. The buns are the limiting reagent; the leftover sausages are the excess reagent; the three hot dogs are the theoretical yield.

  • The amounts of reactants in a mixture might not match the mole ratio, so one can be left over when the other is used up.
  • The limiting reactant is used up completely. It controls the amount of product formed and so sets the theoretical yield.
  • The excess reactant is present in a greater proportion than the mole ratio requires. Some of it is left over at the end.

Example: 1.0 mol H₂ is mixed with 3.0 mol O₂ and ignited. They react 2 : 1, so the reaction stops when the hydrogen runs out.

2H₂(g)O₂(g)2H₂O(l)
ninitial / mol1.03.00
Δn / mol−1.0−0.5+1.0
nfinal / mol02.51.0
  • Initial row: any amounts can be mixed, whatever the coefficients.
  • Change row: the sign shows decrease (reactants) or increase (products). These changes must be in the mole ratio.
  • Final row: nfinal = ninitial + Δn. Like the initial mixture, it is not related to the coefficients.

Extent of reaction

Double the hydrogen (2.0 mol H₂ + 3.0 mol O₂): the oxygen that reacts doubles to 1.0 mol and the water doubles to 2.0 mol. Double the oxygen instead (1.0 mol H₂ + 6.0 mol O₂): nothing changes, 1.0 mol water still forms, because oxygen was already in excess and 5.5 mol is left.

Worked example 2 · calcium carbide16.0 g CaC₂ is heated with 19.3 dm³ O₂ (STP). The oxides then react to form CaCO₃. All reactions go to completion.
CaC₂(s) + 2.5O₂(g) → CaO(s) + 2CO₂(g)
n(CaC₂) = 16.0 ÷ 64.10 = 0.250 mol; n(O₂) = 19.3 ÷ 22.7 = 0.850 mol
Needed 1 : 2.5, present 1 : 3.4 → CaC₂ limiting
Final: O₂ 0.225 mol, CaO 0.250 mol, CO₂ 0.500 mol
CaO(s) + CO₂(g) → CaCO₃(s): 1 : 1, CaO limiting
Final: CaCO₃ 0.250 mol, CO₂ 0.250 mol, O₂ 0.225 mol
m(CaCO₃) = 0.250 × 100.09 ≈ 25.0 g
V(CO₂) = 0.250 × 22.7 ≈ 5.68 dm³; V(O₂) = 0.225 × 22.7 ≈ 5.11 dm³

Reminders: n = m ÷ M (Structure 1.4). Avogadro's law: equal volumes of gases at the same T and p contain equal numbers of molecules, and at STP Vm = 22.7 dm³ mol⁻¹, so n = V ÷ Vm (Structure 1.5).

ActivityCalculate the masses of the initial and final mixtures in worked example 2 and check that mass is conserved.
ATL · solving stoichiometry problems
  1. Formulate and balance the equation(s) for every change in the problem.
  2. Calculate as many amounts as you can with n = m/M and n = V/Vm. Turn a mass percentage into a mass first, then into an amount.
  3. Write the known amounts under the formulas in the equation. Gaps suggest the next step.
  4. Find the limiting reactant and use the mole ratio to work out the changes. The ratio does not give the initial or final amounts.
  5. Check the mass balance: total mass of products = total mass of reactants.
  6. Check the answer makes sense: percentages add to 100%, none is over 100%, and a yield never exceeds 100%. Treat very low or high values with caution.
Try describing each step in three words, then in one.

Finding the limiting reactant quickly

The class method compares the moles you have with the moles the ratio needs. A faster check (useful in Paper 1): divide the moles of each reactant by its coefficient; the smallest answer is the limiting reactant.

Worked example · ethane15 g C₂H₆ reacts with 45 g O₂. 2C₂H₆ + 7O₂ → 4CO₂ + 6H₂O. Mass of water?
n(C₂H₆) = 15 ÷ 30.08 = 0.499 mol → ÷ 2 = 0.249
n(O₂) = 45 ÷ 32.00 = 1.41 mol → ÷ 7 = 0.201 (smaller → O₂ limiting)
n(H₂O) = 1.406 × 6/7 = 1.205 mol → m = 1.205 × 18.02 = 21.7 g
You must find the limiting reactant before choosing which moles to use for the product. The same trick works with gas volumes, since volume ∝ moles (Avogadro's law).
Exam tipExcess left over = moles present − (limiting moles × ratio), then convert to mass.

In Example 1 above (6 g FeCl3, 4 g O2), how many moles of chlorine gas are produced?

FeCl3 is limiting: n = 6 ÷ 162.20 = 0.0370 mol. Ratio FeCl3 : Cl2 = 4 : 6, so n(Cl2) = 0.0370 × 6/4 = 0.0555 mol.

2NaCl + Pb(NO3)2 → 2NaNO3 + PbCl2. What mass of lead(II) chloride forms from 15.3 g NaCl and 60.8 g Pb(NO3)2?

n(NaCl) = 15.3 ÷ 58.44 = 0.262 mol (÷2 = 0.131). n(Pb(NO3)2) = 60.8 ÷ 331.22 = 0.184 mol (÷1 = 0.184). NaCl is limiting. n(PbCl2) = 0.131 mol × 278.1 = 36.4 g. Excess Pb(NO3)2 left: (0.184 − 0.131) × 331.22 = 17.5 g.

2Al + 6HBr → 2AlBr3 + 3H2. 3.22 mol Al reacts with 4.96 mol HBr. Which is limiting, and how much H2 forms?

  1. Al; 4.83 mol
  2. HBr; 2.48 mol
  3. HBr; 4.96 mol
  4. Al; 2.48 mol

Al could give 3.22 × 3/2 = 4.83 mol H2; HBr could give only 4.96 × 3/6 = 2.48 mol. The smaller value wins, so HBr is limiting.

3Si + 2N2 → Si3N4. 21.44 mol Si reacts with 17.62 mol N2. How many moles of Si3N4 form?

  1. 7.15 mol
  2. 8.81 mol
  3. 17.62 mol
  4. 21.44 mol

Si: 21.44 ÷ 3 = 7.15; N2: 17.62 ÷ 2 = 8.81. Si is limiting, giving 7.15 mol.

4FeS2 + 11O2 → 2Fe2O3 + 8SO2. What mass of SO2 forms when 26.62 g FeS2 reacts with 5.44 g O2?

n(FeS2) = 26.62 ÷ 119.99 = 0.222 mol (÷4 = 0.0555). n(O2) = 5.44 ÷ 32.00 = 0.170 mol (÷11 = 0.0155). O2 is limiting. n(SO2) = 0.170 × 8/11 = 0.124 mol; m = 0.124 × 64.07 = 7.92 g. (Rounding to 0.12 mol and using M = 64 too early gives 7.68 g, which is wrong.)

2CuCl2 + 4KI → 2CuI + 4KCl + I2. What mass of iodine forms from 0.56 g CuCl2 and 0.64 g KI?

n(CuCl2) = 0.56 ÷ 134.45 = 0.00417 (÷2 = 0.00208); n(KI) = 0.64 ÷ 166.00 = 0.00386 (÷4 = 0.000964). KI is limiting. n(I2) = 0.000964 mol × 253.80 = 0.24 g.

Multi-step: 3FeCl2 + 2Na3PO4 → Fe3(PO4)2 + 6NaCl. 23 g FeCl2 reacts with 41 g Na3PO4. Find the limiting reagent, the mass of NaCl formed, the excess left over and the % yield if 16.1 g NaCl is collected.

n(FeCl2) = 23 ÷ 126.75 = 0.181 mol; it needs 0.181 × 2/3 = 0.121 mol Na3PO4 = 19.8 g, and 41 g is present, so FeCl2 is limiting. n(NaCl) = 0.181 × 2 = 0.363 mol = 21.2 g. Excess Na3PO4 = 41 − 19.8 = 21 g. % yield = 16.1 ÷ 21.2 × 100 = 76%.

title: Percentage yield
html:
R2.1.4 Conservation of mass

The total mass of the products equals the total mass of the reactants consumed: the law of conservation of mass. Atoms are not created or destroyed, so their total mass cannot change.

Science as a shared endeavour“Nothing comes from nothing” was an ancient Greek principle. The first experimental evidence came in 1748 from the Russian scientist Mikhail Lomonosov, who reacted substances in sealed vessels. His work was almost unknown in western Europe, and Antoine Lavoisier formulated the principle over 25 years later, in 1774, and was commonly credited. How can more scientists' contributions reach the international community?

Percentage yield

Why do we calculate the maximum mass of product? Because that is the theoretical yield, the yardstick against which a real experiment is judged.

Experimental amounts of product are usually lower than predicted, because of incomplete conversion or product lost during isolation and purification.

  • Theoretical yield: the amount or mass of product if the reaction went to completion and none was lost.
  • Experimental yield: the amount or mass actually isolated. It can be equal to or lower than the theoretical yield, but never higher.
percentage yield = experimental yieldtheoretical yield × 100%= nexpntheor × 100% = mexpmtheor × 100%
Worked example 6 · calcium sulfide10.0 g Ca and 9.62 g S produced 17.0 g CaS.
Ca(s) + S(s) → CaS(s)
n(Ca) = 0.250 mol; n(S) = 0.300 mol; n(CaS) = 17.0 ÷ 72.15 = 0.236 mol
Ca limiting → theoretical CaS = 0.250 mol × 72.15 = 18.0 g
% yield = 0.236 ÷ 0.250 × 100 = 17.0 ÷ 18.0 × 100 = 94.4%

Few reactions give a 100% yield. Typical reasons: the reaction is incomplete (some reactant is left, or the reaction is reversible); product is lost during the practical (transfers, filtration, purification, gas escaping); and unwanted by-products form from side reactions. Percentage yield is vital for monitoring the efficiency of industrial processes, where every percent lost is lost profit and extra waste.

Worked example

A reaction between 384 g of sulfur and excess oxygen produced 680 g of sulfur dioxide. Calculate the percentage yield. S + O2 → SO2

  1. n(S) = 384 ÷ 32.07 = 11.97 mol.
  2. Ratio S : SO2 = 1 : 1, so 11.97 mol SO2 could form.
  3. Theoretical yield = 11.97 × 64.07 = 767.2 g.
  4. % yield = 680 ÷ 767.2 × 100 = 88.6%.

What is the % yield of H2O if 138 g H2O is produced from 16.0 g H2 and excess O2? 2H2 + O2 → 2H2O

n(H2) = 16.0 ÷ 2.02 = 7.92 mol → 7.92 mol H2O (1 : 1) → 7.92 × 18.02 = 142.7 g. % yield = 138 ÷ 142.7 × 100 = 96.7%. (With H = 1 and O = 16 you get 144 g and 95.8%; use data-booklet values.)

What is the % yield of NH3 if 40.5 g NH3 is produced from 20.0 mol H2 and excess N2? N2 + 3H2 → 2NH3

n(NH3) = 20.0 × 2/3 = 13.3 mol → 13.3 × 17.04 = 227.2 g. % yield = 40.5 ÷ 227.2 × 100 = 17.8%.

Challenge: 58 g of H2O is produced by combining 60 g O2 and 7.0 g H2. What is the % yield? (Find the limiting reactant first.)

n(O2) = 1.875 mol (needs 3.75 mol H2); n(H2) = 7.0 ÷ 2.02 = 3.47 mol, so H2 is limiting. Theoretical H2O = 3.47 × 18.02 = 62.4 g. % yield = 58 ÷ 62.4 × 100 = 92.9%.

More practice: (a) 12.3 g O2 from 14.0 g H2O (2H2O → 2H2 + O2); (b) 107 g O2 from 300 g KClO3 (2KClO3 → 2KCl + 3O2); (c) 220 g FeS from 3.00 mol Fe; (d) 143 g Fe2O3 from 300 g FeS2 + 200 g O2; (e) mass of Cl2 from 70 g MnO2 + 3.5 mol HCl at 42% yield (MnO2 + 4HCl → MnCl2 + 2H2O + Cl2)

(a) 98.9%. (b) 91.1%. (c) 83.4%. (d) O2 is limiting (6.25 mol, but 2.50 mol FeS2 needs 6.88 mol): theoretical Fe2O3 = 6.25 × 2/11 × 159.70 = 181.5 g, so 78.8%. (e) MnO2 (0.805 mol) is limiting (it needs 3.22 mol HCl): 0.805 × 70.90 × 0.42 = 24 g Cl2.

Data-based: synthesis of aspirin

Salicylic acid (from willow bark) relieves pain and fever but irritates the stomach, so a modified form, acetylsalicylic acid (aspirin), is used. In school, salicylic acid (Mr 138.13) is heated with excess ethanoic anhydride (Mr 102.10) and a few drops of H₃PO₄ catalyst, giving aspirin (Mr 180.17) and ethanoic acid. The crystals are filtered, dried, and purified by recrystallization from hot ethanol. Every step loses some product.

DataExp 1Exp 2Exp 3
salicylic acid / g2.062.572.35
ethanoic anhydride / g2.492.853.11
aspirin / g3.422.311.87
recrystallizationnoneoncetwice
melting point / °C122–128133–135135–136

Pure aspirin melts at 136 °C. Impurities lower the melting point and widen its range (sea water freezes between −2.5 and −1.8 °C, not 0 °C). Aspirin's identity can be confirmed by IR, NMR, mass spectrometry or melting point.

Practical · gravimetric analysis of a precipitate CaCl₂(aq) + Na₂CO₃(aq) → CaCO₃(s) + 2NaCl(aq)
Pre-weigh a labelled filter paper. Mix 25 cm³ of 0.50 mol dm⁻³ CaCl₂ with 15 cm³ of 1.0 mol dm⁻³ Na₂CO₃ in a 100 cm³ beaker and stir. Vacuum filter (Büchner funnel, conical flask, pump), rinsing all precipitate onto the paper. Dry, weigh, and repeat to constant mass.
Safety: eye protection; Na₂CO₃ solution is an irritant, wear gloves.
Questions: limiting and excess reactants; theoretical yield; experimental and percentage yield; compare with classmates; two ways to improve efficiency.

Yield and purity

Chemists balance yield against purity. Medical drugs must be at least 99% pure, so purification lowers yields and raises prices. Detergents or fertilizers can be well below 50% pure if the impurities are safe. In industry, even a small loss of yield costs profit and creates waste that must be disposed of or reused, which is why efficient, low-impact methods (green chemistry) are now widely adopted.

Linking questionWhat errors may cause the experimental yield to be (i) higher and (ii) lower than the theoretical yield?

Why yields fall short

Reasons the experimental yield is less than 100%: the reaction is incomplete (or reversible), side reactions form by-products, and product is lost during transfer, filtration and purification. A "yield" over 100% means the product is impure or still wet.

A student reports a percentage yield of 108% for a dried solid product. What is the most likely explanation?

  1. The reaction made extra product from nothing
  2. The product is still wet or impure
  3. Some product was lost on the filter paper
  4. The limiting reactant was in excess

A yield above 100% is impossible for pure, dry product; trapped solvent or impurities add mass. Losing product would lower the yield.

title: Atom economy and green chemistry
html:
R2.1.5 Green chemistry

Traditionally, efficiency was judged by yield and cost of raw materials, ignoring toxicity, energy use and waste. Green chemistry considers the environmental impact of the whole process and aims to minimize the use and generation of hazardous chemicals.

Common practices: aqueous or solvent-free reactions, renewable starting materials, mild conditions, efficient catalysis, and using any by-products.

Global impact of scienceThe term “green chemistry” was coined in 1991 by American chemists Paul Anastas and John Warner, who set out 12 principles: non-hazardous chemicals and solvents, less energy and waste (“the best form of waste disposal is not to create it in the first place”), renewable materials and accident prevention. These ideas are now in national and international laws.

Atom economy

Hydrogen can be made by passing steam over heated coal: C + 2H2O → 2H2 + CO2. We want the hydrogen; the CO2 is a by-product. All of the carbon goes to waste. Is this efficient?

atom economy = molar mass of desired producttotal molar mass of reaction mixture × 100%
  • The formula is in the data booklet. Include all starting materials, catalysts and solvents in the denominator.
  • A solvent-free A + B → C: atom economy can approach 100% (equal to the yield). A + B → C + D (target C): always well below 100%, because by-product D forms.
  • Solvents and catalysts lower it further: their atoms don't end up in the product.
  • Atom economy is inversely related to the percentage of waste produced.
  • Total mass of products = total mass of reactants, so either can be used in the denominator (at 100% yield).
Worked example 7 · dimethyl carbonateA non-toxic “green” solvent: 4CH₃OH(l) + 2CO(g) + O₂(g) → 2(CH₃O)₂CO(l) + 2H₂O(l)
Reactants: 2 × 90.09 ÷ (4 × 32.05 + 2 × 28.01 + 32.00) × 100% = 83.33%
Products: 2 × 90.09 ÷ (2 × 90.09 + 2 × 18.02) × 100% = 83.33%

Atom-efficient: addition polymerization (Structure 2.4) and hydrogenation of alkenes (Reactivity 3.2): high yields, no solvents, almost no by-products. Inefficient: oxidation of alcohols (R3.2) and electrophilic substitution in aromatics (R3.4, AHL): large volumes of solvent, low yields, sometimes mixtures of isomers.

Percentage yield vs atom economy

Percentage yieldAtom economy
MeasuresHow much product was actually obtainedThe theoretical efficiency of the reaction
Depends onExperimental technique and conditionsOnly the balanced equation
Data neededExperimental mass and theoretical massMolar masses of the desired product and all reactants
Worked example · making hydrogen from coalC + 2H₂O → 2H₂ + CO₂ (H₂ is the desired product)
atom economy = (2 × 2.02) ÷ (12.01 + 2 × 18.02) × 100 = 4.04 ÷ 48.05 × 100 = 8.4%
Counting atoms ("3 of 7 atoms are wasted") is not atom economy: atoms of different elements have different masses, so you must use molar masses.
Exam tipA reaction with one product (e.g. the Haber process) has 100% atom economy but can still have a low percentage yield. Show working even when the answer is obviously 100%.
DefinitionPercentage yield = the actual yield expressed as a percentage of the theoretical yield; it varies with how the experiment is carried out. Atom economy = the theoretical efficiency of a process; it depends only on the balanced equation.

Blast furnace: Fe2O3 + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO2. Calculate the atom economy for iron.

2(55.85) ÷ [159.70 + 3(28.01)] × 100 = 111.70 ÷ 243.73 × 100 = 45.8%.

Ostwald process step: NH3 + 2O2 → HNO3 + H2O. Calculate the atom economy for nitric acid.

63.02 ÷ (17.04 + 64.00) × 100 = 63.02 ÷ 81.04 × 100 = 77.8%.

Zinc carbonate decomposes: ZnCO3 → ZnO + CO2. Calculate the atom economy for zinc oxide.

81.38 ÷ 125.39 × 100 = 64.9%.

(NH4)2SO4(s) + 2NaOH(aq) → 2NH3(g) + Na2SO4(aq) + 2H2O(l). Calculate the atom economy for ammonia.

2(17.04) ÷ [132.17 + 2(40.00)] × 100 = 34.08 ÷ 212.17 × 100 = 16.1%. (Compare the Haber process, N2 + 3H2 → 2NH3: 100%.)

Which statement about the Haber process, N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3, is correct?

  1. Its atom economy is 100% and its yield per pass is also 100%
  2. Its atom economy is 100% but its percentage yield per pass is low
  3. Its atom economy is low because it is reversible
  4. Atom economy and percentage yield are always equal

With a single product every reactant atom ends up in the product, so atom economy is 100%. Being an equilibrium, only about 15% converts per pass; unreacted gases are recycled.

The cost of green chemistry

Green technologies can need expensive equipment, raw materials and recycling facilities, but they cut the costs of environmental remediation, waste management and energy, so in the long run they are commercially attractive. Green processes have greatly reduced emissions of chlorinated solvents and greenhouse gases. Supercritical CO₂ replaces chlorinated solvents in the food industry; biofuel power plants burn renewable fuel.

But some “green” products still need toxic chemicals or lots of energy, and using plant oils or starch takes farmland, reduces biodiversity and raises food prices. A product's greenness must be judged over its entire life cycle, one of the most controversial problems in green chemistry.

ATL · self-managementCreate your own mole-ratio question (reacting masses, or harder with concentrations and gas volumes), write a step-by-step solution, swap with a partner and give “two stars and a wish”.
Linking questionAtom economy and percentage yield both describe efficiency. What other factors should be considered? (Structure 2.4, Reactivity 2.2)

title: Concentration and solutions
html:
R2.1.2 Concentration of solutions

Concentration tells you how much solute is dissolved in a given volume of solution. Dissolve 1 mol (58.44 g) of NaCl and make it up to 1 dm3: the concentration is 1 mol dm−3, or 58.44 g dm−3. Dissolve 5 mol (292.2 g) in the same 1 dm3: 5 mol dm−3, or 292.2 g dm−3. Concentration can be quoted in mol dm−3 (molarity) or in g dm−3; volumes must be in dm3 (divide cm3 by 1000).

c (mol dm−3) = n (mol) ÷ V (dm3) c (g dm−3) = c (mol dm−3) × M

What is the concentration of 1.5 mol of potassium iodide in 150 cm3 of solution?

V = 150 ÷ 1000 = 0.150 dm3. c = 1.5 ÷ 0.150 = 10 mol dm−3.

What volume of 1.5 mol dm−3 sodium chloride solution contains 0.375 mol of NaCl? Give your answer in cm3.

V = n ÷ c = 0.375 ÷ 1.5 = 0.250 dm3 = 250 cm3.

What is the concentration, in mol dm−3, of 1.5 g of KI in 150 cm3 of solution?

Two steps: n = 1.5 ÷ 166.00 = 0.00904 mol; c = 0.00904 ÷ 0.150 = 0.0602 mol dm−3.

What mass of sodium carbonate, Na2CO3, is needed to make 10.0 cm3 of a 0.400 mol dm−3 solution?

n = 0.400 × 0.0100 = 0.00400 mol; m = 0.00400 × 105.99 = 0.424 g. (The formula is Na2CO3, not NaCO3: sodium is +1 and carbonate is 2−.)

Reactions in aqueous solution

Reactions are often done in aqueous solutions (water is the solvent), which are easier to handle and mix than solids and gases. For concentration and volume problems, work in amounts and use the mole ratio.

n = V × cc = nVV in dm³
Worked example 3 · HCl + NaOH1.00 dm³ of 0.500 mol dm⁻³ HCl is mixed with 1.00 dm³ of 0.200 mol dm⁻³ NaOH.
HCl(aq) + NaOH(aq) → NaCl(aq) + H₂O(l)
n(HCl) = 0.500 mol; n(NaOH) = 0.200 mol → NaOH limiting
Final: HCl 0.300 mol, NaCl 0.200 mol; V = 1.00 + 1.00 = 2.00 dm³
[HCl] = 0.150 mol dm⁻³; [NaCl] = 0.100 mol dm⁻³
The water (solvent) is in large excess and is not relevant.
Worked example 4 · absorbing SO₂SO₂ causes acid rain: SO₂(g) + H₂O(g) → H₂SO₃(aq). It can be absorbed by alkali: SO₂(g) + 2NaOH(aq) → Na₂SO₃(aq) + H₂O(l).
2.84 dm³ SO₂ (STP) → 0.125 mol; 2.00 dm³ × 0.400 mol dm⁻³ NaOH → 0.800 mol
0.125 mol SO₂ needs 0.250 mol NaOH → SO₂ limiting
Final: NaOH 0.550 mol, Na₂SO₃ 0.125 mol in 2.00 dm³
[NaOH] = 0.275 mol dm⁻³; [Na₂SO₃] = 0.0625 mol dm⁻³
MeasurementStrictly, volumes of solutions are not additive: the mixture in worked example 3 is 2.01 dm³, about 0.5% more than expected. That is similar to the accuracy of standard volumetric glassware (0.2–0.5%), so we usually treat volumes as additive. When do negligible effects become significant?

Never add the volume of a gas to the volume of a solution. Gases are about 1000 times less dense than aqueous solutions, so absorbing a gas barely changes the solution's volume.

Standard solutions

A standard solution has an accurately known concentration. A primary standard is a substance pure and stable enough to weigh out directly: high purity (about 99.9%), a high molar mass (so weighing errors are a small percentage), low reactivity, and no change in composition in air (it does not absorb water or CO2). Anhydrous sodium carbonate and potassium hydrogen phthalate are common examples. Sodium hydroxide is not: it absorbs water and CO2 from the air. A secondary standard is a solution whose concentration has been found by titrating it against a primary standard; NaOH solution standardized this way can then be used to analyse other solutions.

Making a standard solution (practical)

  1. Weigh the solid in a weighing boat; transfer to a beaker; reweigh the boat and use the difference (or rinse the boat into the beaker).
  2. Dissolve in a minimum of distilled water, stirring with a glass rod (leave enough water for rinsing).
  3. Transfer to a volumetric flask through a funnel; rinse the beaker, rod and funnel into the flask so no solute is lost.
  4. Make up to the graduation mark (bottom of meniscus at eye level), then stopper and invert several times to mix.
Worked exampleMass of Na₂CO₃ for 250 cm³ of 1.75 mol dm⁻³ solution:
n = 1.75 × 0.250 = 0.4375 mol; m = 0.4375 × 105.99 = 46.4 g
Spilling solid on the balance pan (after weighing) lowers the concentration. Overshooting the mark and removing liquid with a pipette also lowers it, because solute is removed with the liquid.

Which substance is the best choice of primary standard?

  1. Solid sodium hydroxide
  2. Anhydrous sodium carbonate
  3. Concentrated hydrochloric acid
  4. Hydrated copper(II) sulfate left in an open dish

Na2CO3 is pure, stable in air and has a reasonably high molar mass. NaOH absorbs water and CO2; concentrated HCl gives off HCl gas, so its concentration is not exactly known.

When making a standard solution, the student overshoots the graduation mark and removes some solution with a dropping pipette. What happens to the concentration?

  1. It is higher than intended
  2. It is lower than intended
  3. It is unchanged, because the volume is now correct
  4. It depends on the temperature

The solution was already too dilute when it overshot; removing some of it removes solute too, so the concentration stays too low. Start again instead.

A scientist then wants to make 250 cm3 of 0.0900 mol dm−3 Na2CO3 from the 1.75 mol dm−3 stock. What volume of stock should be pipetted into the 250 cm3 volumetric flask?

c1V1 = c2V2: V1 = 0.0900 × 250 ÷ 1.75 = 12.9 cm3. Measure it accurately (burette or graduated pipette) into the flask and make up to the mark with distilled water.

Diluting solutions

Adding water does not change the number of moles of solute, so c1V1 = c2V2, where V2 is the total final volume. The volume of water added is V2 − V1.

c1V1 = c2V2 water added = V2 − V1
Worked example

10 cm3 of 1.5 mol dm−3 HCl is diluted to 0.10 mol dm−3. Final volume: V2 = 1.5 × 0.010 ÷ 0.10 = 0.15 dm3. Water to add = 0.15 − 0.010 = 0.14 dm3 (140 cm3).

You add 200 cm3 of water to 300 cm3 of a 2.00 mol dm−3 NaCl solution. Calculate the new concentration.

2.00 × 0.300 = c2 × 0.500, so c2 = 1.20 mol dm−3 (a concentration, so the unit is mol dm−3, not dm3).

What volume of water must be added to 0.50 mol dm−3 HCl to make 400 cm3 of 0.10 mol dm−3 HCl? Answer in cm3.

V1 = 0.10 × 0.400 ÷ 0.50 = 0.080 dm3. Water = 0.400 − 0.080 = 0.320 dm3 = 320 cm3.

Parts per million

Very dilute solutions (pollutants, trace metals) are often given in parts per million (ppm): the mass of solute per million parts of solution. For dilute aqueous solutions, 1 dm3 has a mass of about 1 kg (106 mg), so 1 ppm ≈ 1 mg dm−3. A solution of 1.25 g dm−3 = 1250 mg dm−3 = 1250 ppm; 0.5 mg cm−3 = 0.5 mg ÷ 0.001 dm3 = 500 mg dm−3 = 500 ppm.

Tap water contains 0.0400 g dm−3 of calcium ions. Express this in ppm.

0.0400 g = 40.0 mg, so 40.0 mg dm−3 ≈ 40 ppm.

title: Titration
html:
Titration

How many iron atoms are in an iron nail? Weigh it and use n = m ÷ M: counting by weighing again. For solutions, the equivalent is titration: using a reaction to find the unknown concentration of a solution by measuring exactly what volume of a standard solution reacts with a known volume of it. Most commonly it is a neutralization between an acid and an alkali (a soluble base), which forms a salt and water: H+(aq) + OH−(aq) → H2O(l).

In an acid–base titration, an acid and a base react to form a salt and water. An indicator changes colour when neutralization is complete. If both volumes and one concentration are known, the other concentration can be found from the mole ratio.

Worked example 520.0 cm³ of H₂SO₄ is neutralized by 14.3 cm³ of 0.200 mol dm⁻³ NaOH.
H₂SO₄(aq) + 2NaOH(aq) → Na₂SO₄(aq) + 2H₂O(l)
n(NaOH) = 0.0143 × 0.200 = 0.00286 mol → n(H₂SO₄) = 0.00143 mol
c(H₂SO₄) = 0.00143 ÷ 0.0200 = 0.0715 mol dm⁻³
c₁V₁x₁ = c₂V₂x₂x = coefficients of the two reactants

Carrying out a titration

  1. Prepare the flask: pipette 25.00 cm3 of the alkali into a conical flask using a pipette filler; add a few drops of a suitable indicator.
  2. Prepare the burette: rinse with a little of the acid, fill using a funnel, run some through to clear the air bubble from the jet, remove the funnel, and read the initial volume.
  3. Titrate: stand the flask on a white tile, add acid while swirling, then dropwise near the end point until the colour just changes permanently. Record the final reading.
  4. Repeat: a rough titration first, then accurate runs until you have concordant titres (within 0.10 cm3); average only those.

Titration technique: what earns marks

  • Record burette readings to 2 decimal places, ending in 0 or 5 (e.g. 26.35 cm³). Read the bottom of the meniscus at eye level.
  • Remove the funnel after filling the burette (drips change the reading); run some solution through to clear the air bubble below the tap. A bubble that escapes during the first run makes that titre too large; if that run is excluded the mean is unaffected.
  • Use a white tile and swirl a conical flask (less risk of losing liquid than a beaker).
  • Rinsing the inside of the flask with distilled water returns reagent from the walls and does not change the titre, because it does not change the number of moles of reagent.
  • Repeat until concordant titres (within 0.10 cm³) and average only those. Round the mean to 2 d.p. (e.g. 23.225 → 23.23 cm³).

Calculating the unknown concentration

  1. Sketch the set-up and write down all the volumes and concentrations you know.
  2. Write the balanced equation.
  3. Calculate the moles of the solution whose concentration you know (n = cV).
  4. Use the mole ratio to find the moles of the other reactant.
  5. Divide by its volume to get its concentration.

25.00 cm3 of NaOH is neutralized by a mean titre of 21.30 cm3 of 0.100 mol dm−3 HCl. Calculate [NaOH].

n(HCl) = 0.100 × 0.02130 = 2.13 × 10−3 mol. Ratio 1 : 1, so n(NaOH) = 2.13 × 10−3 mol. [NaOH] = 2.13 × 10−3 ÷ 0.02500 = 0.0852 mol dm−3.

25.00 cm3 of H2SO4 needs 18.40 cm3 of 0.150 mol dm−3 NaOH. Calculate [H2SO4].

n(NaOH) = 0.150 × 0.01840 = 2.76 × 10−3 mol. H2SO4 + 2NaOH, so n(H2SO4) = 1.38 × 10−3 mol. c = 1.38 × 10−3 ÷ 0.02500 = 0.0552 mol dm−3.

An air bubble below the burette tap is not cleared and is ejected during the first titration. What is the effect?

  1. The first titre is too small
  2. The first titre is too large; if that run is discarded, the mean is unaffected
  3. All titres are too large
  4. There is no effect on any titre

The bubble's volume is recorded as if it were liquid delivered, so the first titre is too large. Later runs are fine, and a non-concordant first run is excluded from the mean.

During a titration the inside of the conical flask is rinsed with distilled water. Why does this not change the titre?

  1. Water dilutes the indicator
  2. Water is not a reagent and does not change the number of moles of acid or alkali
  3. Water reacts with the acid
  4. The extra volume is subtracted at the end

Rinsing returns splashes of reagent to the mixture (improving accuracy) without changing the moles present, so the same volume of titrant is needed.

Why remove the funnel after filling the burette, and why use a conical flask rather than a beaker? Answer, then reveal

A drip from the funnel could enter the burette during the titration and change the reading. A conical flask can be swirled with less risk of losing liquid (not just "easier to swirl"). Repeating titrations improves reliability because a single titration could be anomalous.

Back titration

Practical · back titration of eggshells When a substance can't easily be titrated directly, it is first reacted with a known excess of a reagent, and the leftover reagent is then titrated. Eggshells contain CaCO₃, which is insoluble in water. Crushed shells react with excess HCl; the leftover acid is titrated with standard NaOH to find how much acid the CaCO₃ used, and so the mass of CaCO₃.

Equipment: CaCO₃ chips, eggshells, 1.00 mol dm⁻³ HCl and NaOH, phenolphthalein, burette, clamp and stand, conical flasks, drying oven, pestle and mortar, top-pan balance, volumetric pipette and filler, wash bottle, waste containers.
Tasks: design the method and risk assessment, collect enough data, find the % CaCO₃ in each shell, propagate uncertainties, graph with error bars, compare with literature, discuss two errors and improvements.
Linking questionsHow does the molar volume of a gas vary with temperature and pressure? (Structure 1.5) In what ways does Avogadro's law help us describe, but not explain, the behaviour of gases? (Structure 1.4)
Worked example · marble0.188 g marble reacts with 27.20 cm³ of 0.200 mol dm⁻³ HCl (excess). The leftover acid needs 23.80 cm³ of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ NaOH. Find the % CaCO₃.
n(HCl) added = 0.02720 × 0.200 = 5.440 × 10⁻³ mol
n(HCl) left = n(NaOH) = 0.02380 × 0.100 = 2.380 × 10⁻³ mol
n(HCl) reacted with CaCO₃ = 3.060 × 10⁻³ mol
CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂ → n(CaCO₃) = 1.530 × 10⁻³ mol
m(CaCO₃) = 1.530 × 10⁻³ × 100.09 = 0.153 g → 0.153 ÷ 0.188 × 100 = 81.5%
